claim: By default, SQLite runs an automatic checkpoint when the WAL file reaches 1000 pages.
quote: By default, SQLite does a checkpoint automatically when the WAL file reaches a threshold size of 1000 pages.

claim: PRAGMA wal_autocheckpoint sets the auto-checkpoint threshold; zero or negative disables auto-checkpointing.
quote: Setting the auto-checkpoint size to zero or a negative value turns auto-checkpointing off.

claim: All automatic checkpoints run in PASSIVE mode.
quote: All automatic checkpoints are PASSIVE.

claim: The default manual checkpoint style is PASSIVE, which does as much work as it can.
quote: The default checkpoint style is PASSIVE, which does as much work as it can

claim: FULL checkpoints block new writers while pending but do not block new readers.
quote: This mode blocks new database writers while it is pending, but new database readers are allowed to continue unimpeded.

claim: RESTART checkpoints wait until readers use only the database file, ensuring the next writer restarts the log from the beginning.
quote: This ensures that the next writer will restart the log file from the beginning.

claim: TRUNCATE checkpoints truncate the WAL file to zero bytes before a successful return.
quote: it also truncates the log file to zero bytes just prior to a successful return.

claim: A long-running read transaction can prevent checkpoints from completing, causing the WAL file to grow without bound.
quote: then no checkpoints will be able to complete and hence the WAL file will grow without bound.

claim: If another connection holds a read transaction open, the checkpoint cannot reset the WAL file.
quote: If another connection has a read transaction open, then the checkpoint cannot reset the WAL file

claim: A normal checkpoint does not truncate the WAL file unless journal_size_limit is set.
quote: The checkpoint does not normally truncate the WAL file (unless the journal_size_limit pragma is set).

claim: Setting journal_size_limit to zero truncates rollback journals and WAL files to minimum size.
quote: To always truncate rollback journals and WAL files to their minimum size, set the journal_size_limit to zero.

claim: The default journal_size_limit is -1, meaning no limit.
quote: The default journal size limit is -1 (no limit).

claim: BEGIN CONCURRENT lets multiple writers process write transactions simultaneously when the database is in wal or wal2 mode.
quote: The BEGIN CONCURRENT enhancement allows multiple writers to process write transactions simultanously if the database is in "wal" or "wal2" mode

claim: In wal2 mode the system uses two WAL files instead of one.
quote: In wal2 mode, the system uses two wal files instead of one.

claim: In wal2 mode the checkpointer must wait until writers have switched to the other WAL file before checkpointing.
quote: In wal2 mode, the checkpointer has to wait until writers have switched to the "other" wal file before a checkpoint can take place.

claim: In WAL mode, readers do not block writers and a writer does not block readers.
quote: WAL provides more concurrency as readers do not block writers and a writer does not block readers.

claim: In WAL mode, only one writer can be active at a time because there is a single WAL file.
quote: since there is only one WAL file, there can only be one writer at a time.

claim: SQLite allows many simultaneous read transactions from separate connections but only one simultaneous write transaction.
quote: SQLite supports multiple simultaneous read transactions coming from separate database connections, possibly in separate threads or processes, but only one simultaneous write transaction.

claim: In rollback-journal mode, any number of connections can hold SHARED locks at once, allowing many simultaneous readers.
quote: Any number of processes can hold SHARED locks at the same time, hence there can be many simultaneous readers.

claim: In rollback-journal mode, only one EXCLUSIVE lock is allowed on the file and no other lock kind can coexist with it.
quote: Only one EXCLUSIVE lock is allowed on the file and no other locks of any kind are allowed to coexist with an EXCLUSIVE lock.

claim: In rollback-journal mode, a writer that cannot obtain a RESERVED lock fails immediately with SQLITE_BUSY.
quote: In that case, the write attempt fails and returns SQLITE_BUSY.

claim: In rollback-journal mode, a pending writer blocks new SHARED locks while existing readers may finish.
quote: No new SHARED locks are permitted against the database if a PENDING lock is active, though existing SHARED locks are allowed to continue.

claim: In rollback-journal mode, a reader that cannot obtain a SHARED lock fails immediately with SQLITE_BUSY.
quote: If the SHARED lock cannot be obtained, fail immediately and return SQLITE_BUSY.

claim: In rollback-journal mode, no other process can access the database from the time the cache first spills to disk until commit.
quote: no other processes are able to access the database from the time the memory cache first spills to disk until the transaction commits.

claim: BEGIN DEFERRED is the default; a later write in a read transaction either upgrades or returns SQLITE_BUSY.
quote: Subsequent write statements will upgrade the transaction to a write transaction if possible, or return SQLITE_BUSY.

claim: BEGIN IMMEDIATE starts a write transaction immediately and may fail with SQLITE_BUSY if another writer is active.
quote: The BEGIN IMMEDIATE might fail with SQLITE_BUSY if another write transaction is already active on another database connection.

claim: EXCLUSIVE and IMMEDIATE behave identically in WAL mode.
quote: EXCLUSIVE and IMMEDIATE are the same in WAL mode

claim: Upgrading a read transaction to write fails with SQLITE_BUSY if another connection has already modified or is modifying the database.
quote: upgrading to a write transaction is not possible and the write statement will fail with SQLITE_BUSY.

claim: sqlite3_busy_timeout sets a busy handler that sleeps and, after the timeout elapses, causes sqlite3_step() to return SQLITE_BUSY.
quote: the handler returns 0 which causes sqlite3_step() to return SQLITE_BUSY.

claim: Each database connection can have only one busy handler at any given moment.
quote: There can only be a single busy handler for a particular database connection at any given moment.

claim: In WAL mode, a checkpoint cannot reset the WAL while another connection holds a read transaction, so a continuously active reader lets the WAL grow without bound.
quote: no checkpoints will be able to complete and hence the WAL file will grow without bound.

claim: WAL mode can still return SQLITE_BUSY in obscure cases such as exclusive locking mode, last-connection cleanup, or crash recovery.
quote: But there are some obscure cases where a query against a WAL-mode database can return SQLITE_BUSY

claim: synchronous=OFF: SQLite stops syncing once data is handed to the OS; an OS crash or power loss can corrupt the database.
quote: the database might become corrupted if the operating system crashes or the computer loses power before that data has been written to non-volatile storage.

claim: Transactions are durable across application crashes regardless of the synchronous setting or journal mode.
quote: Transactions are durable across application crashes regardless of the synchronous setting or journal mode.

claim: synchronous=NORMAL carries a very small but non-zero chance that a power failure at the wrong moment corrupts the database.
quote: There is a very small (though non-zero) chance that a power failure at just the wrong time could corrupt the database

claim: In WAL mode, synchronous=NORMAL never corrupts the database but does lose durability.
quote: WAL mode is always consistent with synchronous=NORMAL, but WAL mode does lose durability.

claim: A transaction committed in WAL mode with synchronous=NORMAL may roll back after a power loss or system crash.
quote: A transaction committed in WAL mode with synchronous=NORMAL might roll back following a power loss or system crash.

claim: With synchronous=NORMAL in WAL mode, the WAL is synced before each checkpoint and the database file is synced after each completed checkpoint.
quote: the WAL file is synchronized before each checkpoint and the database file is synchronized after each completed checkpoint,

claim: synchronous=FULL in WAL mode is ACID, including durable.
quote: FULL is atomic, consistent, isolated, and durable (ACID) in WAL mode.

claim: In WAL mode with synchronous=FULL, the WAL is synced on every transaction commit; NORMAL omits this sync.
quote: Writers sync the WAL on every transaction commit if PRAGMA synchronous is set to FULL

claim: In rollback-journal mode, synchronous=FULL is not necessarily durable across a power loss.
quote: FULL is not necessarily durable across a power loss in rollback mode.

claim: Without EXTRA, a transaction committed just before a power loss may be rolled back on reboot, though the database does not corrupt.
quote: it is possible that a single transaction that commits right before a power loss might get rolled back upon reboot.

claim: synchronous=EXTRA is FULL plus syncing the directory containing the rollback journal (in DELETE mode).
quote: EXTRA synchronous is like FULL with the addition that the directory containing a rollback journal is synced

claim: synchronous=EXTRA behaves no differently from FULL in WAL mode.
quote: EXTRA is no different from FULL in WAL mode.

claim: In rollback mode, the journal is flushed to nonvolatile storage before any database file changes are made.
quote: to make absolutely sure that all of the rollback journal is safely on nonvolatile storage

claim: A hot journal exists only when an earlier process was in the middle of committing a transaction.
quote: A hot journal only exists when an earlier process was in the middle of committing a transaction

claim: Checkpointing in WAL mode requires sync operations to avoid database corruption.
quote: Checkpointing does require sync operations in order to avoid the possibility of database corruption

claim: WAL mode does not work over a network filesystem because it requires processes to share memory.
quote: All processes using a database must be on the same host computer; WAL does not work over a network filesystem.

claim: The WAL-index shared memory is created by mmapping a file in the same directory as the database, which is the only way SQLite found to ensure processes share it.
quote: create the shared memory by mmapping a file in the same directory as the database itself.

claim: Opening a WAL database requires write privilege on the -shm file if it exists, or write access to the database directory if it does not.
quote: The opening process must have write privileges for "-shm" wal-index shared memory file associated with the database, if that file exists

claim: If the VFS lacks shared-memory methods, opening or converting a database to WAL mode fails.
quote: the attempt to open a database that is already in WAL mode, or the attempt to convert a database into WAL mode, will fail.

claim: Setting EXCLUSIVE locking mode before the first WAL access avoids shared-memory use entirely, so no wal-index shm is created.
quote: If EXCLUSIVE locking mode is set prior to the first WAL-mode database access, then SQLite never attempts to call any of the shared-memory methods

claim: SQLite versions before 3.22.0 could not read a read-only WAL-mode database.
quote: Older versions of SQLite could not read a WAL-mode database that was read-only.

claim: Before burning a database onto read-only media, the database should be switched to journal_mode=DELETE.
quote: it is good practice to convert the database to PRAGMA journal_mode=DELETE prior to burning an SQLite database image onto read-only media.

claim: With always-overlapping readers, checkpoints never complete and the WAL file grows without bound.
quote: then no checkpoints will be able to complete and hence the WAL file will grow without bound.

claim: The SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART and SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE modes can block readers while the checkpoint runs.
quote: The disadvantage of using SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART and SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE is that readers might block while the checkpoint is running.

claim: For transactions larger than about 100 MB, rollback journal modes will likely be faster than WAL.
quote: For transactions larger than about 100 megabytes, traditional rollback journal modes will likely be faster.

claim: For transactions over a gigabyte, WAL mode may fail with an I/O or disk-full error.
quote: For transactions in excess of a gigabyte, WAL mode may fail with an I/O or disk-full error.

claim: In WAL mode, a transaction spanning multiple ATTACHed databases is atomic per database but not atomic across the set.
quote: Transactions that involve changes against multiple ATTACHed databases are atomic for each individual database, but are not atomic across all databases as a set.

claim: In rollback mode, a transaction modifying multiple attached database files updates all of them atomically, using a super-journal.
quote: When multiple database files are modified within a single transaction, all files are updated atomically.

claim: SQLite's documentation warns that exclusive locks used for writes have misbehaved on some network filesystems and caused database corruption.
quote: SQLite relies on exclusive locks for write operations, and those have been known to operate incorrectly for some network filesystems.

claim: The SQLite library is not tested for across-a-network scenarios, so remote database use is at the user's risk.
quote: However, the SQLite library is not tested in across-a-network scenarios, nor is that reasonably possible.

claim: WAL mode is significantly faster than rollback journal in most scenarios.
quote: WAL is significantly faster in most scenarios.

claim: WAL write transactions write content once, whereas rollback-journal transactions write it twice.
quote: Write transactions are very fast since they only involve writing the content once (versus twice for rollback-journal transactions)

claim: WAL uses many fewer fsync() operations than the rollback journal approach.
quote: WAL uses many fewer fsync() operations and is thus less vulnerable to problems on systems where the fsync() system call is broken.

claim: In WAL mode with synchronous=FULL, an additional WAL sync occurs after every transaction commit.
quote: With synchronous=FULL in WAL mode, an additional sync operation of the WAL file happens after each transaction commit.

claim: In WAL mode with synchronous=NORMAL, no sync operations occur during most transactions.
quote: but no sync operations occur during most transactions.

claim: With synchronous=NORMAL in WAL mode, checkpoint is the only operation that issues a sync barrier.
quote: Note that with PRAGMA synchronous set to NORMAL, the checkpoint is the only operation to issue an I/O barrier or sync operation

claim: WAL checkpoints are slower than write transactions, so most commits are fast while checkpointing commits are much slower.
quote: This has the effect of causing most COMMIT operations to be very fast but an occasional COMMIT (those that trigger a checkpoint) to be much slower.

claim: WAL read performance degrades as the WAL file grows, because readers must scan the WAL.
quote: read performance deteriorates as the WAL file grows in size since each reader must check the WAL file

claim: WAL can be slightly slower (about 1-2%) than rollback journal in applications that mostly read and seldom write.
quote: WAL might be very slightly slower (perhaps 1% or 2% slower) than the traditional rollback-journal approach

claim: For transactions larger than about 100 MB, rollback journal modes will likely be faster than WAL, per the official docs.
quote: For transactions larger than about 100 megabytes, traditional rollback journal modes will likely be faster.

claim: Since SQLite 3.11.0, WAL mode handles large transactions as efficiently as rollback mode.
quote: Beginning with version 3.11.0 (2016-02-15), WAL mode works as efficiently with large transactions as does rollback mode.

claim: With synchronous=FULL in rollback mode, the VFS xSync method is used so content reaches disk before continuing.
quote: the SQLite database engine will use the xSync method of the VFS to ensure that all content is safely written

claim: WAL mode with synchronous=NORMAL stays consistent but loses durability, so committed transactions may roll back after power loss.
quote: WAL mode is always consistent with synchronous=NORMAL, but WAL mode does lose durability.

claim: The SQLite docs describe synchronous=NORMAL as providing the best balance of performance and safety for most WAL applications.
quote: The synchronous=NORMAL setting provides the best balance between performance and safety for most applications running in WAL mode.

claim: In a secondary-source benchmark (10,000 autocommitted inserts), throughput rose from about 279 to about 33,135 inserts/s moving from default DELETE+FULL to WAL+NORMAL.
quote: a single experiment that logged roughly 279 inserts per second jumps to about 33,135 inserts per second on the same drive.

claim: In the same secondary-source benchmark, WAL with synchronous=FULL reached only about 442 inserts/s.
quote: WAL with synchronous=FULL only reaches about 442 inserts per second, barely better than the baseline
